content.text:
Operator
Greetings, and welcome to Installed Building Products Fiscal 2024 Q2 Financial Results Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A brief question-and-answer session will follow the formal presentation. If anyone should require operator assistance during the conference, please press star zero on your telephone keypad. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce your host, Darren Hicks, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.
Darren Hicks
VP of Investor Relations, Installed Building Products
Good morning, and welcome to Installed Building Products Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Earlier today, we issued a press release on our financial results for the second quarter, which can be found in the investor relations section of our website. On today's call, management's prepared remarks and answers to your questions may contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the federal securities laws. These forward-looking statements are based on management's current expectations and beliefs. These statements are subject to risks, uncertainties, and other factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from those described today. Please refer to the cautionary statements and risk factors in our SEC filings, including our annual report on Form 10-K. We undertake no duty or obligation to update any forward-looking statement as a result of new information or future events, except as required by federal securities laws.
In addition, management refers to certain non-GAAP and adjusted financial measures on this call. You can find a reconciliation of such measures to the nearest GAAP equivalent in the company's earnings release and additional reconciliation for EBITDA and adjusted EBITDA for earlier fiscal years in our investor presentation, which are available on our investor relations section of our website. This morning's conference call is hosted by Jeff Edwards, our Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, and Michael Miller, our Chief Financial Officer, and joined by Jason Niswonger, our Chief Administrative and Sustainability Officer. I will now turn the call over to Jeffrey.
Jeffrey Edwards
Chairman and CEO, Installed Building Products
Thanks, Darren. Good morning to everyone joining us on today's call. As usual, I will start the call with some highlights and then turn the call over to Michael, who will discuss our financial results and capital position in more detail before we take your questions. During Q2, we began the process of winding down the operations of a single branch that installed non-core building products into newly constructed commercial structures. We believe that excluding the financial results of this branch from our typical income statement metrics is useful in understanding and evaluating the results of our ongoing operations as it is non-core. As such, all income statement figures mentioned on this call exclude the aforementioned branch results and are thus net of dispositions.
Our Q2 sales results continue to reflect fundamental improvements in our single-family end market relative to the last 12 months and good sales growth in our multifamily end market. We believe our customers are committed to meeting new construction homeownership demand by continuing to build new single-family homes in the current macroeconomic backdrop. We expect our multifamily backlog to keep branches in core geographic markets busy in the near term, despite ongoing industry headwinds as it relates to multifamily unit starts. Longer term, we believe opportunities in our multifamily end markets remain attractive. I'm encouraged by the positive same branch sales growth we achieved in our single-family end market. The nearly 8% year-over-year increase during the quarter was the strongest increase in same branch sales since Q4 2022.
Single-family sales growth was supported by a growing proportion of sales from national production builders in the quarter. Our deep customer relationships, local market knowledge, and ability to align our pricing with the value we offer our customers were key to our Q2 single-family sales results. Our multi-family installation sales growth continued to be resilient with the apparent operational benefits of our centralized service-oriented model. On a same branch basis, multifamily sales in our installation segment increased 5%. In addition, across our branches, there continues to be an opportunity to sell IBP's installation services in our markets that historically have not served multifamily customers. The sales growth results for our commercial installation segment reflect different dynamics in the two submarkets that make up our commercial end market.
The heavy commercial market continues to experience healthy growth, while our light commercial market continues to experience some headwinds as the light commercial construction cycle tends to lag single-family construction activity. Excluding dispositions, commercial sales growth was modestly positive in the quarter. Strong profitability during Q2 continued to reflect our strategic priority to apply our local market expertise to efficiently complete the most operationally and financially attractive jobs for our local business. As a result, our Q2 adjusted EBITDA margin expanded to 18.5%. Acquisitions continue to be our top priority as we consider all of our options for capital allocation. Despite our growth over the years, we believe a meaningful opportunity still exists for us to expand our geographic presence and diversify the mix of building products we install across our national branch network.
During the 2024 Q2 and in July, we completed the following acquisitions: a North Carolina-based installer of insulation and other diversified building products, serving single-family and multifamily customers with annual revenue over $6 million. An Oklahoma-based installer of insulation and a Massachusetts-based installer of gutters with combined annual revenue of approximately $14 million. An Illinois-based installer of a diversified set of building products with annual revenue of approximately $20 million. To date, we have acquired over $50 million of annual revenue, and we expect 2024 to be another favorable year of acquisition growth. We believe we are well positioned for another year of strong operational and financial performance in 2024 as we continue to focus on profitability and effective capital allocation to drive earnings growth and value for our shareholders.
Based on the U.S. Census Bureau, single-family starts year-to-date through June 2024 have increased by 16%. We believe the current pace of starts growth supports a healthy market environment for our single-family installation services. Additionally, beyond the typical demand drivers, we believe the United States government incentives and plan mandates towards more stringent energy efficiency standards in new and existing single-family homes will be favorable for our business. We intend to continue to focus on what we can control, leveraging our strong customer relationships, experienced leadership team, national scale, and diverse product categories across multiple end markets to help the company navigate through any future changes in the U.S. construction market. I'm proud of our team's continued success, commitment to excellence, and ability to consistently meet the needs of our customers.
To everyone at IBP, thank you for your commitment, your hard work, and a tough job always done well. I remain excited by the prospects ahead for IBP and the broader insulation and other product installation business. With this review, I'd like to turn the call over to Michael to provide more detail on our Q2 financial results.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Thank you, Jeff, and good morning, everyone. As Jeff noted earlier, all income statement references in my comments are net of dispositions. Consolidated net revenue for Q2 increased 8% to $740 million, compared to $687 million for the same period last year. The increase in sales during Q2 was driven by growth in our new and existing residential markets. Our single-family same branch sales increased 8%, while our multifamily same branch sales increased 5% during Q2.
Although the components behind our price mix and volume disclosure have several moving parts that are difficult to forecast and quantify, we continue to experience top-line improvement from a 6.4% increase in price mix during Q2, which more than offset modestly lighter job volumes down 1.4% relative to Q2 last year. Our business achieved strong results in Q2 as measured by an adjusted gross margin of 34.9%, adjusted net profit margin of 11.6%, and adjusted EBITDA margin of 18.5%. Adjusted selling and administrative expense as a percent of Q2 sales was 18.3% due to higher variable compensation related to higher gross profit and EBITDA performance from the prior year period.
Within that result, administrative expenses, excluding variable compensation in Q2 2024, was flat with Q1 2024. Adjusted EBITDA for 2024 Q2 increased 11.3% to a record $136.6 million, and adjusted EBITDA margin improved to 18.5% compared to 17.9% for the same period last year. We continue to target full-year long-term same branch incremental adjusted EBITDA margins in the range of 20% to 25%. For 2024 Q2, total same branch incremental adjusted EBITDA margin was 29%. Adjusted net income per diluted share improved 14.5% to $3.02 per share.
Although we do not provide comprehensive financial guidance based on recent acquisitions, we expect Q3 2024 amortization expense of approximately $10 million and full-year 2024 expense of approximately $42 million. We would expect these estimates to change with any acquisitions we close in future periods. Also, we continue to expect an effective tax rate of 25% to 27% for the full year ending 31 December 2024. Now, let's look at our liquidity position, balance sheet, and capital requirements in more detail. For the six months ended 30 June 2024, we generated $164 million in cash flow from operations compared to $138 million in the prior year period.
The year-over-year increase in operating cash flow was primarily associated with higher net income and effective management of working capital. Our second quarter net interest expense decreased to $8.2 million from $9.8 million in the prior year period, primarily due to a greater amount of interest income from higher interest rates on higher balances of cash and cash equivalents relative to the year ago period. At 30 June 2024, we had a net debt to trailing twelve-month adjusted EBITDA leverage ratio of 0.97 times compared to 1.32 times at 30 June 2023, which is well below our stated target of 2 times. At 30 June 2024, we had $355 million in working capital, excluding cash and cash equivalents.
Capital expenditures and total incurred finance leases for the three months ended 30 June 2024 were approximately $22 million combined, which is approximately 3% of revenue, roughly in line with the same period last year. With our strong liquidity position and modest financial leverage, we continue to expand the business through acquisition and return capital to shareholders. During 2024 Q2, IBP repurchased 215,000 shares of its common stock at a total cost of $46 million. At 30 June 2024, the company had over $250 million available under its stock repurchase program. IBP's Board of Directors approved the Q3 dividend of $0.35 per share, which is payable on 30 September 2024 to stockholders of record on 15 September 2024.
The Q3 dividend represents a 6% increase over the prior year period. With this overview, I will now turn the call back to Jeff for closing remarks.
Jeffrey Edwards
Chairman and CEO, Installed Building Products
Thanks, Michael. I'd like to conclude our prepared remarks by once again thanking IBP employees for their hard work, dedication, and commitment to our company. Our success over the years is made possible because of you. Operator, let's open up the call for questions.
Operator
Thank you. We will now be conducting a question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. A confirmation tone will indicate your line is in the question queue. You may press star two if you would like to remove your question from the queue. For participants using speaker equipment, it may be necessary to pick up your handset before pressing the star keys. Your first question comes from Stephen Kim with Evercore ISI. Please go ahead.
Stephen Kim
Senior Managing Director and Head of Housing Research, Evercore ISI
Thanks very much, guys. Thanks for all the color. Excuse me. But as usual, we have additional questions. I guess my first one was, if you could speak to any verticals that maybe slowed a little bit in the quarter that's worth calling out or maybe missed your internal projections, you know, any verticals. Then broadly, when we think about fiberglass, curious if you could talk about how the price pass-through is going. My sense is it's going well, but wanted to get your sense and then also what you think the potential is for a third increase this year.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Stephen, good morning. This is Michael. On the first part of that question relative to the verticals, I would say that, you know, all lines of business, all end markets performed very much in line with our expectations. As we had highlighted in previous quarters, clearly the weakest part of the business right now is the light commercial business, with which naturally cycles behind single-family development. We would expect as we go into the latter half of this year and early part of next year, given the strength that we've seen in single-family, that that business would start to recover. I would say that across the board, the business performed as expected from a revenue perspective and actually performed better than we expected from a gross margin perspective. I don't know if you want to talk about that.
Jeffrey Edwards
Chairman and CEO, Installed Building Products
Yeah. Stephen, hi, this is Jeff. You know, in terms of the material tightness and pricing, it is still a very, you know, tight market. We expect it to continue to stay that way probably through the end of the year. You know, obviously it's an environment in which manufacturers have been able to realize price, and it's one in which we, you know, try to at least make up the ground that we need to make up. You know, I can speculate as to whether there's a third one or not. It's a little late in the year, I suppose. Maybe I won't speculate.
Stephen Kim
Senior Managing Director and Head of Housing Research, Evercore ISI
Okay, great. That's fine. I guess, Mike, you talked a little bit about the, you know, the incentive comp. I assume that was maybe weighing a little bit on the incremental organic incremental EBITDA margin. Just wondering if there was anything else maybe to call out 'cause that came in a little lower than we were expecting. With respect to the HUD mandate on single family, you know, the energy code HUD mandate, which is coming next year, I guess I'm just curious to hear if you could address that and your thoughts around that. We've been getting questions as to whether or not we might see FHFA follow on.
There's been also questioning around whether or not all of this just may disappear, you know, maybe due to the Chevron, you know, the ruling around the Chevron. I don't know what the word is, but you know what I mean by the Chevron case. The potential for a Republican sweep maybe to just undo all this. Just curious if you could talk about the HUD mandate broadly.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
I mean, as far as we know, and as far as everything that we've heard, that, you know, the process is continuing. You know, we believe that there might be some pushback relative to the timing of implementation, but it's very difficult for us to speculate what would happen in a, you know, change in the political environment. As far as we know, and as far as our customers are working, we're all sort of working towards this getting put in place. You know, ultimately, it still benefits the builder because they have the tax credit that will more than offset the cost of going to the '21 energy code. That I think everyone believes is gonna stay, and will still continue to be available. It does make economic sense for them and obviously for the homeowner as well.
We think regardless of the political outcome, you know, that logic and economics will continue to push forward getting more builders building to the '21 energy code. In terms of your margin question, you know, adjusted gross margin and both adjusted EBITDA margin and all of our comments, our net of dispositions, you know, were very strong from our perspective, quite frankly. You know, the SG&A adjusted SG&A leverage, you know, that was higher. I should say the, you know, the costs that were higher on a relative basis to revenue was really all driven by variable compensation. If you look at it on a three-quarter basis, basically, that number has been quite in line for the past three quarters as a percentage of revenue.
If you look at just G&A dollars, excluding variable compensation, right, they've been flat for the past couple of quarters.
Jeffrey Edwards
Chairman and CEO, Installed Building Products
The only thing I'd like to add on the 2021 code is, I mean, backing up from the politics for a moment, it wasn't created just kind of willy-nilly. It's created because, you know, it's good for the environment and saves energy ultimately. It's been well known that from in terms of insulation as kind of the payback as it relates to home energy costs and kind of the effects of you know against the environment, that insulation is probably, if not, the most effective way to combat some of those things. It's certainly you know up there in the top tiers.
Stephen Kim
Senior Managing Director and Head of Housing Research, Evercore ISI
Okay, great. Thanks very much, guys.
Jeffrey Edwards
Chairman and CEO, Installed Building Products
Sure.
Operator
Next question, Adam Baumgarten with Zelman & Associates, please go ahead.
Adam Baumgarten
Managing Director, Zelman and Associates
Hey, guys. Thanks for taking my questions. First on multifamily, just kind of how we think about the back half of the year. It's decelerated a bit, but still positive. Maybe do you expect positive same store sales growth in multifamily in the back half at this point?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Well, Adam, as you know, we don't provide guidance. I would say a couple of things on the multifamily side. The, you know, the backlogs are still at a highly elevated level. One of the things that we look at are units under construction relative to starts. If you look at that on a single family basis, it's currently running somewhere around 7 to 8 months, which is consistent with kind of long-term trends sort of pre-COVID. We would say that cycle times have completely normalized in single family, maybe even improved a little bit above normal in the single-family construction market. On multifamily, as I think everybody on the call is probably aware, the units under construction or the backlog continues to be quite elevated.
You know, normal in that market would be more like 20 to 23 months of starts. Currently, it's running around 28 to 29 months of starts. You know, construction or units under construction still need to come down probably 25 to 30% to normalize given the current starts level. You know, that creates a significant headwind for the industry and for us. You know, we feel good about our ability to continue to gain market share and improve the cross-sell of other products in multifamily. Clearly, that significant a readjustment in the units under construction is going to have an impact on our multifamily sales.
I would say that the, what's maybe changed from our perspective relative to that is we think that the normalization of the units under construction is gonna happen sooner than we may have expected, say, 3 to 6 months ago. That also means that we'll come to a stabilization period sooner than we had expected, meaning that we will be able to then focus on just continuing to gain market share and seeing revenue growth in multifamily from market share gains, versus overall market growth. That was a long-winded way of not answering your question, but because we don't provide guidance.
I do think, Hugh, that, you know, there is a good chance that if multifamily units under construction comes in for the full year between 600,000 and 700,000 completions, that we will get to that more normalized 20 to 23 months, which in essence then creates a stable operating environment for multifamily construction.
Adam Baumgarten
Managing Director, Zelman and Associates
Okay, got it. No, that's helpful. Then just on the disposition, maybe just a little more color on what that non-core product line was. If we think about the rest of your footprint, any other opportunities or plans for additional dispositions?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Absolutely not. All of our other branches are performing, you know, to our expectations or even exceeding our expectations. This was a one-off deal that, obviously in hindsight, we wish we hadn't done. It is a non-core product. We really don't install it in any of our locations, and it was into the commercial and multifamily vertical. You know, the good news is it's behind us now.
Adam Baumgarten
Managing Director, Zelman and Associates
Okay. Thank you.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Yeah.
Operator
Next question, Michael Rehaut with JPMorgan, please go ahead.
Michael Rehaut
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst at JPMorgan Chase & Co, JPMorgan
Hi. Thanks. Good morning, everyone.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Good morning.
Michael Rehaut
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst at JPMorgan Chase & Co, JPMorgan
Wanted to hit first on the gross margins. You know, you're talking about basically, you know, last 4 or 5 quarters now, plus or minus 34%, which is, you know, solidly above your, I think long-term or longer term goal, you know, where I think, you know, 32%, you know, that I guess long-term outlook, 30 to 32. It seems like you're, you know, consistently exceeding that. I think a quarter or two ago, you know, you kind of alluded to likely strength in this metric, perhaps, you know, continued strength around these levels, maybe, you know, through the end of this year. Again, not giving forward guidance, but basically kind of saying there's no drivers that would necessarily, you know, push this down materially from current levels in the near term, at least.
I was wondering if that is still your thought around this metric, that, you know, this 34% level can persist. I know you've talked about maybe negative mix starting to eat away at this metric. You know, any thoughts around, you know, the next several quarters, what might push it lower? Or do you feel perhaps a little increasingly comfortable that this level can be maintained in the near to medium term?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Yeah, thanks. Thanks for that question. What I would say around gross margin is that, you know, adjusted gross margin in the quarter net of dispositions was 34.9%, so I'll just call it 35%. You're right, in the previous quarters, we've been running around 34%. We certainly don't expect it to go above the 35%. To say for the near term and, you know, really for the back half of the year, for it to be more in a 32% to 34% range as opposed to the 30% to 32%, I think is reasonable. You know, we have had in the quarter, quote-unquote "mix headwinds" as we've talked on multiple quarters about the impact of the growth in production builder business.
I would say that, you know, we've been doing an excellent job, improving the efficiency of completing jobs for the production builders, which has been helping, you know, gross margin improvement as it relates there. You know, we had very strong growth with the production builders in the quarter. Our sales to the production builders was up approximately 20% in the quarter and about 5% with the regional and local builders, which is actually consistent with what we've been talking about, that, you know, the regional and local guys were gonna have a good year, but nothing in comparison to what the production builders had, and that the vast majority of the growth and starts would be coming from the production builders. We're certainly seeing that play out.
I think it's reasonable to assume that, you know, for the near to medium term, that the, you know, there's certainly going above the 35% is probably not likely, but staying in a 32% to 34% range for the near to medium term is reasonable.
Michael Rehaut
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst at JPMorgan Chase & Co, JPMorgan
Great. Great. No, that's very helpful. Appreciate that. I guess second question, maybe just around the M&A backdrop. You've kind of highlighted, you know, doing about $50 million in annualized revenues so far year to date. Last year, you kind of, you know, missed the $100 million target by a little bit. You know, how would you characterize the pipeline and the opportunity set in front of you today maybe versus six or 12 months ago. You know, I think if I recall right, you kind of reiterated the $100 million outlook for this year. What would you say the odds are of maybe exceeding that and, you know, is the M&A kind of outlook or pipeline increasing, decreasing, you know, staying the same?
You know, any kind of change in how you're thinking about, you know, what you might do this year or next year?
Jeffrey Edwards
Chairman and CEO, Installed Building Products
Yeah. This is Jeffrey. What I would say, I know we're guilty of saying it's robust all the time, but we're also guilty of saying that they're lumpy. Really versus 6 or 12 months ago, this is, and versus really, historically speaking, one of the best pipelines we've really ever had. You know, but for a larger deal, you know, $30+ million that blew up at the last part of last year, last year would have ended up being a pretty good year, too, at least certainly exceeding the $100 million. You know, going forward, again, we feel really great about the prospects that are in the pipeline and the deals that are kind of even already signed up to LOI. It just depends on timing, really.
You know, I guess if you look at all of it over a long, you know, rolling period of time as opposed to counting calendar days, you'll probably still hit the numbers.
Michael Rehaut
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst at JPMorgan Chase & Co, JPMorgan
Yeah.
Great. Thanks so much.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Sure.
Operator
Next question, Mike Dahl with RBC Capital Markets, please go ahead.
Mike Dahl
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, RBC Capital Markets
Hi. Thanks for taking my questions. Just on the price mix in the quarter, I know there's a lot of moving pieces and it's hard to be too specific, but can you give us a ballpark sense of kind of the composition of true price versus the moving pieces on mix?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
We definitely got price in the quarter. You know, given the acceleration in single family, same branch revenue, being higher than multifamily, same branch revenue, just when factoring in those two components, you know, the way that our price mix is determined, it would say that we got more price than we did mix because of the higher growth rate from single family.
Mike Dahl
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, RBC Capital Markets
Okay. Helpful. Just back on the disposed branch, I mean that as a standalone, it seemed like there were maybe some issues in terms of kind of negative net revenue, negative adjusted EBITDA, pretty big negative adjusted EBITDA that then you're adding back. I think you called it the process of winding down, then also said it's behind you. Maybe just say, like, a little more specifically on why the results were so pressured, 'cause that was kind of a big adjustment to the total company results. Secondly, on a go-forward basis, are there still going to be lingering impacts into the second half here? Just any additional color you could provide would be helpful.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Yeah, we expect that the operations will be fully wound down by the beginning of next year. That going forward, it will have a material impact. Immaterial, excuse me, very important distinction there. An immaterial impact on our results going forward. Part of the reason that the adjustments were so large in this quarter is because we made the decisions to dispose of the location and, you know, kind of take care of and clean up all of the issues that were there. This is again a non-core branch completely out of anything else that we do that has, quite frankly, never been profitable.
Mike Dahl
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, RBC Capital Markets
I'm hesitant to even call it a branch. I mean, really, it's a product line.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Yeah. From a branch perspective.
Mike Dahl
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, RBC Capital Markets
Yeah. I think sure, it's located in a branch, but.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Right.
Mike Dahl
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, RBC Capital Markets
More than that, we're exiting a product line in which we don't really participate.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Exactly. Quite frankly, we've done over 200 acquisitions. This is the first time this has happened. I think that's a pretty darn good track record.
Mike Dahl
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, RBC Capital Markets
Just as a quick follow-up, since it's being backed out of EBITDA but not gross margin and SG&A, does that imply that the way you report adjusted gross margin and SG&A would have otherwise been higher? If you could give us a sense for if that was part of the reason that your SG&A was higher than expected. Like, did more of the costs flow through that? Yeah, any sense of that breakdown?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
It was just the table. I mean, we wanted to try and make it concise enough in terms of the tables that we put in to show the adjustment. As I said in answer to a previous question, the adjusted gross margin in the quarter, excluding dispositions, would have been 34.9%. It impacted. It negatively impacted basically all lines of the income statement.
Mike Dahl
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, RBC Capital Markets
Okay. Got it. I had missed that comment. Thank you.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Great.
Operator
Next question, Reuben Garner with The Benchmark Company. Please go ahead.
Reuben Garner
Analyst, The Benchmark Company
Thank you. Good morning, guys.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Good morning.
Reuben Garner
Analyst, The Benchmark Company
Sorry to harp on this, but just a clarification on the commercial front. Is the run rate of revenue and profit loss that's being stripped out in Q2 the right way to think about on a go-forward basis, meaning it added $7 million EBITDA to take that business out? Was it losing that much money on a quarterly basis?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
It lost that much money in Q2, yes. It is commercial. Our same branch commercial revenue, excluding the disposition, was basically flat in Q2 and not negative.
Reuben Garner
Analyst, The Benchmark Company
Okay. You guys typically compare your volume performance to kind of the completions-
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Yeah
Reuben Garner
Analyst, The Benchmark Company
-environment for the two end markets. You guys are, you know, not quite national yet. There's some MSAs that you're not in. Is there anything geographical that you would call out, that may lead to differences between your performance and the completions environment, broadly?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
No, I'm glad you asked that question, though, because I think it's important, and we've tried to stress this, is that looking at our same branch revenue compared to completions in any one quarter is not as impactful or useful as looking at it over a longer period of time. If you look on the year-to-date for the first six months of the year, our same-brand sales grew, you know, 4.7, so call it 5%, and multi-family or single-family completions were up about 1%, right? That delta of about 400 basis points, that's sort of mid-single digit, is very consistent with what we've always talked about sort of being at a mid-single digit number above completions.
I will say on the multifamily side right now that, one, as you know, over the past, you know, several, more than several quarters, we've had stellar growth in, same branch multifamily sales growth. I would say just given the dynamics of what we were talking about earlier about multifamily units under construction, there is going to be, for some period of time, I think, a disconnect between our multifamily same branch sales growth and multifamily completions until the market normalizes at a more, reasonable level, which we think, you know, in terms of the units under construction relevant to starts, which we think is gonna happen, you know, maybe late this year, most likely Q1 of next year.
Reuben Garner
Analyst, The Benchmark Company
If I could just sneak in a quick follow-up there, guys. The multifamily impact to mix on a go-forward basis as single family, you know, recovers and multifamily fades, can you just remind us how that plays out?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
It makes the mix component weaker. It's a headwind to the mix because a single-family job, you know, can be a tenth of or even a hundredth of what a multifamily job is.
Reuben Garner
Analyst, The Benchmark Company
Great. Thanks, guys. Good luck going forward.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Thanks.
Operator
Next question, Kenneth Zener with Seaport Research Partners, please go ahead.
Kenneth Zener
Analyst, Seaport Research Partners
Good morning, everybody.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Morning, Kenneth.
Reuben Garner
Analyst, The Benchmark Company
Morning.
Kenneth Zener
Analyst, Seaport Research Partners
Just a couple of questions here. Given the strength of growth from the large builders, and your, I guess, record gross margin adjusted, can you talk to why that is not a drag, as that happened, you know, in the beginning of the pandemic, given your exposure to certain customers? It seems to be somewhat counterintuitive. Can you talk to why that is playing out that way?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Our field team is doing an incredible job of managing production and making sure they are aligning the value of our services, you know, with our customers. You know, to be honest with you, that gets reflected then in variable compensation, and they're getting rewarded for continuing to do that.
Kenneth Zener
Analyst, Seaport Research Partners
Going back to the period when you had, you know, increased exposure and gross margin, you called it out, you know, SG&A leverage at the time. Like, you know, you talked about not wanting to mess up your customers' pricing structure. Jeferey, I believe you talked about going after price given that experience. It seems that large builders, you get leverage. However, there's really two of you guys that are so dominant in the service, you know, installation space. Does that really suggest that your pricing discipline, i.e. margins, is sustainable in that sense if they don't have a wide variety of, you know, bids to choose from? Because it does seem to be a rather distinct shift, especially this quarter, given the growth we're seeing from publics and your actual stronger gross margins because of that.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Well, This is Michael. I'll start that and Jeff can finish it. There are a lot of puts and takes into, you know, gross margin. While we had strong growth with the big public builders, and they are our largest customers, I mean, it is a relatively small percentage of our overall revenue. You know, I would also say that at the local level, there's not just two contractors that are bidding for work. I mean, it's still an extremely competitive environment.
I would say all builders, whether they're publics or regional and local builders, have choices, and we all have to differentiate ourselves on service.
Kenneth Zener
Analyst, Seaport Research Partners
All right.
Jeffrey Edwards
Chairman and CEO, Installed Building Products
I mean, I know I think I understand the question, but I'm gonna still give a bit. I mean, I know our answer that says that we get rewarded for performing is a little fuzzy. I mean, I've been in the rooms, and there are certain bigger builders that do, you know, I think really believe that and preach that to their people even more than others, let's say. Does it mean we get, you know, in more highly price-only competitive situations sometimes? For sure. There's just as many large builders in, too, some of our larger markets that are much more concerned about making sure that they get jobs insulated and pass inspections when they need them to keep the volume.
Kenneth Zener
Analyst, Seaport Research Partners
Understood. Michael, you said, you know, it could be understood that you got more price than mix, given that that's reported a little differently than one of your peers. Is that to say, you know, my calculation, is that to say price was positive and mix perhaps was negative? Could you comment on just the positive, negative component of that variable?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Both price and mix were positive, right? If we look at, you know, my comment was really more that there was more price than mix, but they were both solid.
Kenneth Zener
Analyst, Seaport Research Partners
Thank you.
Operator
Next question, Philip Ng with Jefferies. Please go ahead.
Philip Ng
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Hey, guys. Your commentary on going forward still sounds pretty upbeat. Certainly, housing starts have been a little choppier the last few months.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Yeah.
Philip Ng
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
with rates staying a bit more elevated. Now, certainly we're talking about potential rate cuts. I'm just curious, what are you hearing from your customers? You know, are they managing their business any differently? Are you seeing any slowdown in quoting activity at all?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Yeah, we're still very busy. I mean, I think it's clear that the growth rate in starts is coming down. You know, the publics that have reported so far, I think their orders are up like 5, 6%. Still growth, but not the kind of growth that we were seeing earlier in the year. I mean, honestly, a mid-single digit, single-family growth environment is extremely healthy for us and for the industry. If we continue a multiyear path in that kind of a market, we feel very good about our ability to perform. You know, clearly there are significant headwinds, as we talked about earlier, relative to multifamily.
If we do get to a stabilized level, you know, based on the current starts, you know, say early 2025 as opposed to even back half of 2025, we think that creates a more stable operating environment for us and for the industry. On the multifamily side, again, really allows us to focus on what we're doing very well, is gaining market share, not just with insulation, but also with the other products.
Jeffrey Edwards
Chairman and CEO, Installed Building Products
I was gonna make that comment, too. I mean, we're just we're a little different than just the general multifamily market, as we said in our prepared remarks, both 'cause we're not penetrated, you know, from a geographic perspective everywhere that we are capable of doing multifamily work yet. We continue through one of our operations that, you know, has kind of built itself into a bidding, quoting, and managing machine for those branches, continues to really, you know, deliver a great pipeline of projects that we can bid on and hopefully get the work from.
Philip Ng
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Gotcha. Michael, appreciating you don't guide, per se, but I think, earlier conversations in the year, perhaps mid-single digit volume growth for your business organically, I think your comments were, seems plausible and achievable. You know, appreciating there's a lag in starts and completion, cycle times and all that great stuff. Are you expecting volumes to kinda inflect? You know, what kind of path do you see? Is that mid-single digit framework still a good way to think about it for the full year?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Yeah. If we just look at, say, single family. Single family volumes in the quarter were up mid-single digits.
Philip Ng
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Okay. In terms of the broader framework, in terms of your demand overall, is that still a good way to think about the year or maybe some moderation just given some of the chop that we've seen recently?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Yeah. I mean, from a volume perspective, where we're gonna find some headwinds will be particularly in the light commercial business. You know, we expect that the light commercial business will continue to have headwinds really, you know, again, through the back half of this year and should be on a much better footing in 2025.
Philip Ng
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Okay. Can you remind us, like, how much of your commercial business is light versus heavy, the splits?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Sure. You know, roughly 10% of total revenue is light commercial and 7% is heavy commercial.
Philip Ng
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Okay. Appreciate the color, guys.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Yep.
Operator
Next question, Susan Maklari with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.
Susan Maklari
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Thank you. Good morning, everyone.
Jeffrey Edwards
Chairman and CEO, Installed Building Products
Morning, Susan.
Susan Maklari
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
My first question is on the ancillary products. Can you talk a bit about how they performed in the quarter? That's something that you've talked about increasingly coming through in the back half of this year. Are we still on track with that? Just how should we think about the implications that we'll have from a margin perspective as we think about the upcoming next several quarters?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Yeah. The sales growth in the other products was you know fairly consistent with insulation. Although insulation was you know a tad. They were consistent, I would say. We would expect that the other products would see just becoming later in the cycle time, that they would see probably higher growth than insulation. I would say, though, that you know the story, if you will, relative to the other products as it relates to the you know residential piece of our business, so single-family, multifamily, new residential piece of our business, that we're continuing to make progress in improving the gross margin in those products. They're still you know considerably lower than insulation, but you know we're continuing to make forward progress there.
It's one of the reasons why, you know, we think in the near to medium term, as we were saying earlier, that, you know, gross margins, you know, will probably not grow from here. Being in a 32 to 34 band in the near term probably makes some sense.
Susan Maklari
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Okay. My follow-up is you did buy some stock this quarter.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Yeah.
Susan Maklari
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
I think this was the biggest repurchase you've had since 2022. Can you just talk a bit about the decision to do that and how we should be thinking about perhaps further share buybacks over the in the future?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Yes, we will continue to do it. We believe that as we continue to mature as a public company and we continue to generate very strong free cash flow, that it gives us a lot of opportunities, if you will, from a capital allocation perspective. You know, we feel very confident that we can currently support an even accelerated M&A platform or pipeline of deals, you know, above our $100 million target and at the same time continue to repurchase shares on a more consistent basis.
Susan Maklari
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Okay. Thank you, and good luck with everything.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Thanks, Susan.
Operator
Thank you.
Next question, Keith Hughes with Truist Securities. Please go ahead.
Keith Hughes
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Truist Securities
Thank you. Just some details on this branch you're getting out of. Are there gonna be any appreciable asset sales that you would anticipate from this move to close it?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
No, nothing significant. We really expect for the back half of the year, until it's fully disposed, that it'll have an immaterial impact on results going forward.
Keith Hughes
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Truist Securities
I assume that would include EBITDA. There's something about an unfavorable contract settlement in the language of the press release. Was that all taken care of in the quarter?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Correct.
Keith Hughes
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Truist Securities
there's no impact in the second half?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Correct. That's the reason why the quarterly EBITDA contribution was so negative.
Keith Hughes
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Truist Securities
Okay. Can you tell us what product line this is, as you're getting out? I know it's non-core, but specifically what?
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
It's non-core.
Keith Hughes
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Truist Securities
Your discussion on share repurchase, I know you did some in the quarter. Have you thought internally about, in excess of the dividend, how much would go that way? How, I guess, how are you thinking about it, is the question.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Yeah. I mean, if you look over the past, say, 5 years and from a capital allocation perspective, roughly 60% or almost $550 million went to acquisitions and, you know, 20% or almost $200 million went to share repurchases, and then about $160 million went to the dividend. I think, as we've said, the number one priority will continue to be M&A, then share repurchases, and then the dividend.
Keith Hughes
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Truist Securities
Okay. Thank you.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
As we said in answer to Sue's question, it's our belief that, you know, we will be more consistent in regular share repurchases on a go-forward basis.
Keith Hughes
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Truist Securities
Okay. Thank you.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Sure.
Operator
I would like to turn the floor over to Jeff Edwards for closing remarks.
Michael Miller
CFO, Installed Building Products
Thank you for your questions, and I look forward to our next quarterly call. Thank you.
Operator
This concludes today's teleconference. You may disconnect your lines at this time, and thank you for your participation.

content.text:
Operator
Good day everyone and welcome to the Installed Building Products Fiscal 2024 Q1 Financial Results Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. Later, you will have the opportunity to ask questions during the question and answer session. You may register to ask a question at any time by pressing the star and one on your telephone keypad. You may withdraw yourself from the queue by pressing star and two. Please note today's call is being recorded, and I'll be standing by if you need any assistance. It's now my pleasure to turn the conference over to Darren Hicks, Managing Director of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.
Darren Hicks
Managing VP of Investor Relations, Installed Building Products
Good morning and welcome to Installed Building Products First Quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Earlier today, we issued a press release on our financial results for Q1, which can be found in the investor relations section of our website. On today's call, management's prepared remarks and answers to your questions may contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the federal securities laws. These forward-looking statements are based on management's current expectations and beliefs. These statements are subject to risks, uncertainties, and other factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from those described today. Please refer to the cautionary statements and risk factors in our SEC filings, including our annual report on Form 10-K. We undertake no duty or obligation to update any forward-looking statement as a result of new information or future events, except as required by federal securities laws.
In addition, management refers to certain non-GAAP and adjusted financial measures on this call. You can find a reconciliation of such measures to the nearest GAAP equivalent in the company's earnings release and additional reconciliation for EBITDA and adjusted EBITDA for earlier fiscal years in our investor presentation, which are available on our investor relations sections of our website. This morning's conference call is hosted by Jeff Edwards, our Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, and Michael Miller, our Chief Financial Officer, and joined by Jason Niswonger, our Chief Administrative and Sustainability Officer. I will now turn the call over to Jeff.
Jeffrey Edwards
President, CEO, and Chairman, Installed Building Products

You know, it's gonna be, there are a lot of puts and takes there, but I mean, it's something that's gonna add, call it, you know, over time, 5%, 10%, 20% revenue to that overall branch.
Jeffrey Edwards
President, CEO, and Chairman, Installed Building Products
Well, theoretically, it is possible to have the same share in those products.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
It is.
Jeffrey Edwards
President, CEO, and Chairman, Installed Building Products
In some markets, we overperform in those products, you know, in the products other than insulation.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Right.
Jeffrey Edwards
President, CEO, and Chairman, Installed Building Products
I guess the other comment I'd make is, when you closed out your question, Ken, you said as an M&A strategy. I would say this is as much of an organic growth strategy, probably more than it is an M&A strategy.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
In a lot of ways.
Jeffrey Edwards
President, CEO, and Chairman, Installed Building Products
In a lot of ways.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Yeah. When it's an M&A strategy, it's a real small tuck-in acquisition that then grows the organic opportunity.
Jeffrey Edwards
President, CEO, and Chairman, Installed Building Products
Not always, but a lot of times.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Yeah.
Ken Zener
Senior Analyst, Seaport Research Partners
All right. Appreciate that. Then I know you touched on fiberglass price trends a little bit, but with volume recovery, can you talk about the potential upside, downside related to tight supply, and how you feel you're mitigating potential risks of having to go to, you know, third-party supplier channels if, you know, volume increases, again?
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Yeah
Ken Zener
Senior Analyst, Seaport Research Partners
We don't see any margin surprises.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Yeah. I mean, we actually, you know, I think we learned a lot of lessons from the last couple of years in terms of just how tight material was and the stress that it caused on the organization. We've done a lot of things internally to improve our operational efficiency in terms of material management and material ordering, and also working very closely with our suppliers to make sure that we're as efficient as we can in terms of getting the materials that we need. You know, we feel very good about our ability to do that and to manage the process. You know, are things tight and are they probably gonna get tighter, particularly as the single family continues to ramp up? Yes.
You know, we think some of the investments we've made in people and procedures around that have really improved our ability to mitigate the necessity of going to alternative sources for particularly fiberglass.
Jeffrey Edwards
President, CEO, and Chairman, Installed Building Products
It doesn't mean there aren't hiccups, though.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Right. Of course.
Jeffrey Edwards
President, CEO, and Chairman, Installed Building Products
I mean, we still have that. To Michael's point, I guess, a combination of Jeff Heyer and actually, Brad Wheeler, our COO, who was not at the time our COO, were kind of juggling this ball, and we've added a wingman. Neither one of them now are having to handle it. We've got a guy full-time kind of playing traffic cop as it relates to fiberglass.
Ken Zener
Senior Analyst, Seaport Research Partners
Could you perhaps be a little more specific, realizing, you know, if there's a secret sauce, you don't wanna give it away. But from the outside, if supply is tight, you know, you just couldn't get it or is it that you're bidding more in line with your known supply? Could you expand a little bit? Thank you very much.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Yes. We are, you know, as we've talked at numerous occasions, you know, we always want to value our services properly and align that with an appropriate amount of volume. An appropriate amount of volume comes with knowing what our supply is going to be and making sure we're focusing on servicing the customers that are our highest priority. It is a question of just understanding, you know, where supply is gonna be and what the volume of work we wanna do.
Jeffrey Edwards
President, CEO, and Chairman, Installed Building Products
I would say this, that supply, though, is definitely not curtailing our bidding activity.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Yeah
Jeffrey Edwards
President, CEO, and Chairman, Installed Building Products
Landing jobs for those jobs that we want to bid.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Exactly
Jeffrey Edwards
President, CEO, and Chairman, Installed Building Products
want to get.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Yeah.
Jeffrey Edwards
President, CEO, and Chairman, Installed Building Products
Right.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
It's an important clarification.
Ken Zener
Senior Analyst, Seaport Research Partners
Thank you.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Mm-hmm.
Operator
Our next question will come from Mike Dahl with RBC Capital Markets.
Mike Dahl
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, RBC Capital Markets
Morning. Thanks for taking my questions. Can I go back to the mix dynamic a little bit? I just wanna be clear because I understand the narrative and expectation for the production builder mix. Quite frankly, if we look at starts growth on the single family side, it's not all that different than what the public builders are reporting. It does seem like the privates are actually holding their own better than a lot of people might have thought.
In your quarter and what was reflected in the gross margin in the quarter, were you already seeing a meaningful shift towards production builders, or that's something that you're still starting to talk about as kind of a prospective, haven't seen it yet, but keep in mind, we still do expect this through the year and into next year?
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Yeah. I think there's two-part answer to that question. We saw the inflection towards production builders in January, and we're continuing to see that inflection. It's our belief that while the starts being up 27% in Q1 is sort of reflective of backlogs and orders from the builders, starts, right, would be fully reflective not just of orders or backlogs, but also spec, right? So the spec building shows up in starts, but it doesn't show up in backlogs and orders. So as a consequence, it's our belief that the production builders, which are the ones that are heavy spec, their starts numbers are stronger than what they're reporting, right? Because of that, specs don't show up in really much of anything other than permits and starts, right?
Obviously completions and sales when it comes to the end, right? From our perspective, what you're seeing in backlog and order reporting from the builders is somewhat understating what the level of starts that they're creating at this time because of that spec inventory. We again, but I don't wanna dismiss the importance of the regional and local builders because they're still building along at a good pace. It's just that they're not accelerating at the rate that the production builders are.
Mike Dahl
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, RBC Capital Markets
Okay. Yeah. Got it. I mean, I hear you. Yeah, it seems like the privates might be holding on a little bit better. Not that that's a bad thing, right? I just from a margin standpoint wanna make sure that-
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Yeah
Mike Dahl
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, RBC Capital Markets
Setting. And then on the multifamily dynamic, you know, units under construction did just inflect negative. I think if we look at the rate of kind of starts versus completions and run that out, like you're probably gonna be in a position where units under construction are, you know, into Q4 and into 2025, down, you know, 20%, then 2025 probably down 25-30% in terms of under construction. So I know that it's due with a lag, but again, from kind of a level setting exercise, when you talk about challenges next year, what environment are you thinking about as far as your baseline for how much of a headwind that could be to you?
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Well, I think the macro environment is definitely going to have a significant headwind similar to, you know, what your thinking is, right? We would expect that multifamily, certainly from a permits and starts perspective, is going to normalize to historical trends, this year, right? It already is. Although permits in Q1, for multifamily have averaged about 430, which, you know, arguably is above trend. We would expect that, you know, going into 2025 in the first part, you know, certainly Q1, you're still going to have some carryover of the units under construction. You know, I think the whole industry is going to be facing a market in 2025 that looks more like what, you know, multifamily has looked like for the 10 years prior to COVID.
That's honestly a very good environment for us to be in. Clearly, it's an adjustment for the market to go through. What we believe and what gives us a lot of optimism is it's happening at the same time that single family is accelerating in the right direction. Again, you know, single family is by far our largest end market at 60% and multifamily is, you know, 15%, 16%, 17%. We feel very good about the ability of the single family strength to offset the headwinds on the multifamily side. As we said earlier, our ability to perform above the market opportunity by gaining market share in multifamily, particularly through the cross-selling of other products.
Mike Dahl
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, RBC Capital Markets
Okay, thanks for that.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Sure.
Operator
Our next question will come from Jeffrey Stevenson with Loop Capital.
Jeffrey Stevenson
VP of the Equity Division, Loop Capital
Hi, thanks for taking my questions today, and congrats on a nice quarter.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Great. Thank you.
Jeffrey Stevenson
VP of the Equity Division, Loop Capital
Mike, you talked about opportunities for multifamily share gains in 2025 from expanding your successful centralized model from your CQ Insulation acquisition in key IBP markets. How long will it take to get this centralized model for things like bidding, labor, and payments across your branch footprint? Do you have a long runway?
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
We do have a pretty long runway. You know, there are plenty of our markets that don't use CQ or have the benefit of CQ that are already have great, you know, relationships and multifamily market penetration. So we would never put that model into those markets. We would let them to continue to be kind of independent, if you will, of the CQ model, so to speak. But the team at CQ has identified markets that have great opportunity for them, where we have strong single family market share and, you know, low or weak multifamily market share. They're working on performing on that strategy each and every day. They're making incremental progress every single month on expanding their sort of bidding and managing network within that identified portion of our footprint.
Jeffrey Stevenson
VP of the Equity Division, Loop Capital
That's right.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
You know, it's really.
Jeffrey Stevenson
VP of the Equity Division, Loop Capital
Okay.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
It's really a, you know, if we make a smaller acquisition in a market, let's say, that we weren't in, it's a matter of kind of growth of the branch, really.
Jeffrey Stevenson
VP of the Equity Division, Loop Capital
Yeah.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
You know, it's really a labor thing. You know, one of the gentlemen that's been in the business for a long time that works for us, one of his sayings is He who has the labor wins, right? You know, if you have the work, you can get the labor, but if you get the work, you've got to get the labor. It's just, it takes a little bit of time, but that's really the kind of play that we're running with CQ in those markets.
Jeffrey Stevenson
VP of the Equity Division, Loop Capital
Okay, great. No, that's good color. I was wondering if you could talk about the opportunity with spray foam over the coming years, given the long-term industry demand tailwinds from changes in building codes, and then on top of that, the tight fiberglass supply environment.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Yeah. It's our belief that, you know, particularly if the whole country doesn't effectively go to the 2021 energy code, that it will definitely mean greater penetration of spray foam. It's yet to fully be seen exactly what that will look like, whether it's a hybrid home that's, you know, part fiberglass, part spray foam. You know, we do think that fiberglass will continue to remain the dominant product for residential insulation, but we definitely can see a pathway towards greater usage of spray foam. To be clear, you know, spray foam is the most technical thing that we install, and it requires the highest trained installers that we have. It also requires fairly expensive equipment that is on a very long lead time.
As a consequence, you can't just flip the switch overnight and then convert things to spray foam. It is a transition, and it takes time, which is why, you know, we think the way that the FHA, VA, and potentially Fannie and Freddie coming in and requiring install to the 2021 energy code being pushed out, if you will, to, you know, probably 2025, 2026 is constructive because it gives the industry time to size up, if you will, for this new spray foam opportunity.
Jeffrey Stevenson
VP of the Equity Division, Loop Capital
Great. Thank you.
Operator
Our next question will come from Keith Hughes with Truist.
Keith Hughes
Managing Director of Sell-Side Equity Research, Truist
Thank you. Just back to multifamily real quick. You gave your view of the market, which has been pretty consistent in terms of units. I guess on margin, the margin your competitors are recording in multifamily was just extremely high, given it was such a hot market. That's obviously gonna come off. Can you quantify or directionally give us what is that part of, you know, your future mix and what that could potentially do to margins or EBITDA?
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Yeah. I mean, our team has done a great job of maintaining the margin profile within the work that we're bidding. I mean, clearly, as the market gets tighter, there'll, you know, continue to be some pressure there. You know, our team is doing an excellent job of really identifying the right jobs, the right opportunities, and making sure that we get paid for the value that our services provide. You know, I would say that, you know, there have been a couple of questions around this. You know, we have consistently talked about full year adjusted gross margins in that 30% to 32% range. Admittedly, we have been consistently for multiple quarters above that level.
You know, our thinking long term relative to that 30% to 32%, really is informed by, one, this growth in production builder business that we've been talking about, and that, you know, multifamily, you know, again, as it goes back to a more normalized level of, call it, you know, 300,000 to 400,000 units, there will probably be some level of pricing pressure there. Our team has done an excellent job of resisting that, and, you know, I think our performance in that business, demonstrates their ability to be successful.
Keith Hughes
Managing Director of Sell-Side Equity Research, Truist
Okay great. Thank you.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Sure.
Operator
Our next question will come from Phil Ng with Jefferies.
Colin Lalevee
Equity Research Associate, Jefferies
Hey good morning. This is actually Colin on for Phil. Thank you for taking my question. I just wanted to go to price mix. It was strong in the quarter, especially with that mix headwind from the production builder side. I guess, just, with the manufacturers announcing the price increases, any color as to how those conversations have gone for you to your customer base going forward? Should we expect the contribution from pricing to really build into Q? Any color there as to how you're thinking about pricing going forward?
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Yeah. When we think about the quarter, I mean, it seems like a long time ago, but the, you know, the market did take price, material price increases in Q1. Obviously, which I think our team has done a great job of doing is, you know, we're trying to match, selling price, install price with that increase in material price, which then comes through the price/mix calculation. To the extent that, and as Jeff said, we think that there's, you know, material continues to be tight. It's a little early to tell what's gonna happen with this next announced price increase. You know, we will work with our customers to make sure that there's a fair balance between rising material prices and, where we're going from an install price perspective.
Now, that being said, we would continue to expect price to be positive as we go through the year. It's just the mix component that will weigh on the price/mix because, you know, obviously, we had a strong performance in multifamily same-branch sales growth in the quarter, but it is decelerating from the rates that we saw in previous quarters. As single family production builder business ramps up and takes the reins of growth, if you will, from multifamily, that will, you know, impact negatively the price/mix, the mix component of the price/mix calculation.
Colin Lalevee
Equity Research Associate, Jefferies
Great. Thank you for the color and good luck for the rest of the year.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Thank you.
Jeffrey Edwards
President, CEO, and Chairman, Installed Building Products
Thank you.
Operator
Our next question will come from Adam Baumgarten with Zelman & Associates.
Adam Baumgarten
Managing Director, Zelman & Associates
Hey good morning, guys.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Good morning.
Adam Baumgarten
Managing Director, Zelman & Associates
You talked about residential same branch growth accelerating year to date. Have you seen maybe on a monthly basis, positive year over year volumes in single family at this point?
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Yeah. I mean, you may or may not know, April was a weird month because it had 2 extra selling days in it. Even adjusting for those 2 extra selling days, you know, we felt very good about the single-family growth in April.
Adam Baumgarten
Managing Director, Zelman & Associates
Okay got it. Just on the manufacturer price increases, you know, we've got two effectively this year so far. Do you expect further increases maybe in the H2 of the year at this point with given the tightness?
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
If Jeff Heer were in the room and able to answer, he would probably say something along the lines of, they may not be able to help themselves. There probably is inflationary, you know, pressures still. Is there a chance? Yes, I think so.
Adam Baumgarten
Managing Director, Zelman & Associates
Okay got it. Just lastly for me, just anything weather-wise that impacted the quarter negatively and maybe pushed some of the volume out into subsequent quarters?
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Yeah, I mean, you know, weather in January and February was a little challenging, but March was much better. I would say nothing of significance that really moved volume one way or another.
Adam Baumgarten
Managing Director, Zelman & Associates
Okay great. Thanks. Best of luck.
Michael Miller
EVP, CFO, and Director, Installed Building Products
Sure.
Operator
That will conclude today's question and answer session. I'll now turn the call over to Jeff Edwards for any additional closing remarks.
Jeffrey Edwards
President, CEO, and Chairman, Installed Building Products
Thank you for your questions, and I look forward to our next quarterly call. Thank you.
Operator
This does conclude today's program. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
